title: Olympic Basketball
text:
How did player ages differ across men’s basketball teams at the 2016 Olympics? I used TidyTuesday data from August 6, 2024 to compare the teams.
The full data cover the Olympics from 1896 to 2016. RGriffin put the Sports Reference records on Kaggle. I kept the men’s basketball event in 2016. This gives 141 players from 12 teams. Each player has one row and an age.
library(tidyverse)

olympics <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-08-06/olympics.csv')

basketball <- filter(olympics, sport == "Basketball", year == 2016, sex == "M")
Each box shows the middle half of a team’s ages. The line in the box marks the median.
ggplot(basketball, aes(x = age, y = team)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(
    title = "Player ages by team",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Team"
  )
China has the lowest median age at 22.5 years. Brazil has the highest at 31. The United States falls between them at 26. Argentina has a wide age range, from 21 to 39.
The records list 10 players for Croatia and 11 for Nigeria. Each other team has 12. These comparisons use the players in the data.

title: Who gets mentioned in Suits?
text:
Who gets mentioned the most in Suits episode summaries? Does that change from season to season?
This project uses 134 episode summaries from TVmaze, covering all nine seasons. I checked for six characters by first name. A name counts once per summary, even if it shows up more than once. This tells us who the summaries mention. It doesn’t tell us how much screen time they get.
Each of the 134 rows is one episode, not a line of dialogue. The five original variables are id (episode ID), name (episode title), url (episode page), airdate, and summary (a short description of the episode). The dataset contains summaries, not full scripts or dialogue. I use the episode URL to identify the season and the summary to check for character names.

title: Who gets mentioned in Suits?
text:
Get the data ready

library(tidyverse)

suits <- read_csv("data/suits_episodes.csv")

suits <- suits |>
  mutate(
    text = str_replace_all(summary, "<[^>]+>", " "),
    text = str_to_lower(text),
    season = str_extract(url, "(?<=suits-)\\d+(?=x)")
  )


suits <- suits |>
  mutate(
    Harvey = str_detect(text, "\\bharvey\\b"),
    Mike = str_detect(text, "\\bmike\\b"),
    Louis = str_detect(text, "\\blouis\\b"),
    Donna = str_detect(text, "\\bdonna\\b"),
    Jessica = str_detect(text, "\\bjessica\\b"),
    Rachel = str_detect(text, "\\brachel\\b")
  )

mentions <- suits |>
  select(season, Harvey, Mike, Louis, Donna, Jessica, Rachel) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = Harvey:Rachel,
    names_to = "character",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  )

title: Who gets mentioned in Suits?
text:
Who gets mentioned the most?
I first compare all six characters to see whose names appear most often across the episode summaries. Counting summaries rather than every mention keeps a name repeated within one summary from adding extra weight.

overall <- mentions |>
  group_by(character) |>
  summarise(episodes = sum(mentioned))

ggplot(overall, aes(x = episodes,
                    y = fct_reorder(character, episodes))) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Harvey gets mentioned the most",
    x = "Summaries with their name (out of 134)",
    y = "Character"
  )








Harvey is first with 123 of the 134 summaries. Mike is next with 96, followed by Louis with 86. Rachel has 50, Jessica has 45, and Donna has 39. Some characters stay on the show longer, which gives them more chances to show up in a summary.

title: Who gets mentioned in Suits?
text:
Does this change by season?
The overall totals can hide changes as characters enter or leave the show. I compare Harvey, Mike, and Louis across seasons to see whether their prominence in the summaries stays consistent. I use percentages because seasons have different numbers of episodes.

by_season <- mentions |>
  filter(character %in% c("Harvey", "Mike", "Louis")) |>
  group_by(season, character) |>
  summarise(
    episodes = n(),
    mentions = sum(mentioned),
    percent = 100 * mentions / episodes
  )

ggplot(by_season,
       aes(x = season, y = percent, color = character,
           group = character)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Harvey, Mike, and Louis by season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Summaries with their name (%)",
    color = "Character"
  )








Some seasons have more episodes than others, so I used percentages to compare them. Harvey is in at least 80% of the summaries in every season. Mike has the biggest drop. He is in every summary in season 7, none in season 8, and two of the ten in season 9. Louis is at his highest in seasons 6 and 7, with 15 of the 16 summaries in each.
Mike’s drop fits a change in the cast: Patrick J. Adams left the regular cast after season 7 and returned as a guest in season 9, according to USA Network. This helps explain why Mike disappears from the season 8 summaries and appears again in season 9. It also shows why the totals need context: fewer summary mentions can reflect a character leaving the show, rather than becoming less important while still appearing regularly. A summary can also leave out a character who appears in the episode, so mentions are not a direct measure of screen time.

title: Who gets mentioned in Suits?
text:
Where the data came from

TVmaze contributors. (n.d.). Suits episode information and summaries. Retrieved October 14, 2026, from the episode list and episode data API.
The CSV file uses selected fields from TVmaze’s data. The data are shared under CC BY-SA 4.0. See TVmaze’s licensing terms.

title: Movie Budgets
text:
Do films with bigger budgets earn more at the box office? I used TidyTuesday data from October 23, 2018 to look at film budgets and ticket sales. The data come from The Numbers.
I removed one repeated row and kept films with box office totals above zero. This leaves 3,364 films from 1936 to 2018. The dollar amounts do not account for inflation.
library(tidyverse)

movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2018/2018-10-23/movie_profit.csv')

movies <- select(movies, movie, release_date, production_budget, worldwide_gross)
movies <- distinct(movies)
movies <- filter(movies, worldwide_gross > 0)
Each point shows one film. Both axes use millions of US dollars.
ggplot(movies, aes(x = production_budget / 1000000,
                  y = worldwide_gross / 1000000)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Movie budgets and box office revenue",
    x = "Production budget (US$ millions)",
    y = "Worldwide box office (US$ millions)"
  )
Films with bigger budgets tend to bring in more at the box office, but the points spread out. Films with close budgets can have very different ticket sales. Minions, for example, had a budget of $74 million and brought in about $1.16 billion worldwide.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text: Does spending a larger share of the payroll on three players go along with better team performance? To look at this, I will find how much of each MLS club’s guaranteed compensation goes to its three highest-paid players. Using data from 2020 to 2026, I will compare average expected goal difference per match for clubs with higher salary concentration and clubs with lower salary concentration. I will then shuffle the performance values to see whether the difference could reasonably show up by chance.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text: Does spending a larger share of the payroll on three players go along with better team performance? To look at this, I will find how much of each MLS club’s guaranteed compensation goes to its three highest-paid players. Using data from 2020 to 2026, I will compare average expected goal difference per match for clubs with higher salary concentration and clubs with lower salary concentration. I will then shuffle the performance values to see whether the difference could reasonably show up by chance.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text:
Understanding the data
The salary data come from the MLS Players Association (MLSPA), through American Soccer Analysis (ASA). ASA also provides the expected goals data. Each salary row is a player listed for a club in one season’s release; each performance row is a club-season pairing, such as NYCFC in 2025. I join them using team ID and year.
Guaranteed compensation includes base salary and annualized guaranteed bonuses and other guaranteed compensation. It differs from the budget charge, the amount counted toward the league salary budget. I measure salary concentration as the three highest-paid players’ combined compensation divided by total club compensation. These players are not necessarily official designated players (DPs).
Expected goals (xG) measure scoring-chance quality using estimated probabilities that shots become goals. Expected goals conceded measure the chances allowed to opponents. Expected goal difference per match (xGD per match) is xG for minus xG against, divided by matches played. This covers attack and defense while accounting for different numbers of matches.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text:
Make the two groups
I average salary concentration and xGD per match across each club’s available seasons, giving each season equal weight. This leaves one row per club instead of treating its repeated seasons as independent observations. I split clubs at the median salary share, using salary data alone to decide the groups.


Code
clubs <- club_seasons |>
  group_by(team_id, team_name) |>
  summarize(salary_share = mean(top_three_share),
            performance = mean(xgd_per_match),
            seasons = n(), .groups = "drop")

cutoff <- median(clubs$salary_share)
clubs <- clubs |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(salary_share > cutoff,
                        "Higher concentration", "Lower concentration"))

group_summary <- clubs |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarize(clubs = n(), mean_xgd = mean(performance), .groups = "drop")
group_summary


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  group                clubs mean_xgd
  <chr>                <int>    <dbl>
1 Higher concentration    15 -0.0196 
2 Lower concentration     15  0.00769


Code
observed_difference <- mean(clubs$performance[clubs$group == "Higher concentration"]) -
  mean(clubs$performance[clubs$group == "Lower concentration"])


There are 198 club-season records and 30 clubs. The dividing salary share is 40.3%; clubs above it are in the group with higher salary concentration, and clubs at or below it are in the group with lower salary concentration. These labels are relative to this dataset, not official MLS categories. Clubs have between 2 and 7 seasons of coverage.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text:
How do the groups compare?
I use a boxplot to see whether performance differs between the two groups. Each point is one club, showing the spread of performance within each group.


Code
ggplot(clubs, aes(x = group, y = performance)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Do clubs with more concentrated salaries perform differently?",
       subtitle = "Each point is a club average over available 2020-2026 seasons",
       x = "Top-three salary concentration group",
       y = "Average expected goal difference per match") +
  theme_minimal()









Higher points represent clubs that create better chances than they allow. The table above gives the group means, while the plot shows how much club performance varies around them. The observed difference, calculated as higher concentration minus lower concentration, is -0.027 expected goals per match.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
section: Compare the result with the null distribution
text:
Compare the result with the null distribution
The histogram shows differences in means from the shuffled datasets, with the observed difference marked in red. For the two-sided p-value, I count simulated differences at least as far from zero as the observed one.


Code
ggplot(null_results, aes(x = difference)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_difference, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Differences in performance under the null hypothesis",
       subtitle = "Red line: observed difference in group means",
       x = "Mean xGD per match: higher minus lower concentration",
       y = "Number of simulations") +
  theme_minimal()









The simulated p-value is 0.7259. In other words, about 72.6% of the shuffled datasets produced a difference at least as far from zero as the actual one. This describes how unusual our statistic is under the null model; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
section: What this can and cannot tell us
text:
What this can and cannot tell us
These observational data cannot show that salary concentration causes performance to change. Total payroll, player quality, coaching, and injuries could also matter. Splitting clubs at the median also loses some detail about their salary shares.
The simulation assumes performance values can be shuffled between groups under the null. This is an approximation because clubs play each other and have different years of coverage. The shorter 2020 season and partial 2026 season also limit the comparison. The findings describe the MLS clubs and seasons in these files, rather than all soccer clubs or future seasons.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text:
Conclusion
I compared MLS clubs using the share of guaranteed compensation paid to their three highest-paid players and their average expected goal difference per match. I divided clubs into the two salary concentration groups and used a function with map_dbl() to simulate 10,000 shuffled differences in means. The observed difference was -0.027 expected goals per match, and the simulated two-sided p-value was 0.7259. At a 0.05 cutoff, this does not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null model, while the observational data and uneven season coverage limit what we can conclude about roster strategy.

title: MLS Salary Concentration and Team Performance
text:
Sources

Salary data: MLS Players Association Salary Guide, retrieved through American Soccer Analysis. The latest available release within each year was retained; records without team IDs or compensation were excluded.
Performance data: American Soccer Analysis, the source of expected-goals estimates and regular-season team aggregates.
Data links: ASA player salary data, example for 2024, ASA regular-season team xG data, example for 2024, and ASA team names and IDs. The salary and performance requests were repeated for 2020-2026. The input CSV files are stored in this website’s data folder.
Methods: Class notes: permutation tests, especially the two-sample test using shuffled outcomes, differences in means, and repeated simulations.
